A file reopened from the archive (2004, closed for ‘insufficient evidence’):

· Complainants: P. Doyle-Hart and Q. Bui. Subject: the shipyard’s discharge of solvent into the river.
· The sample bottles handed in as evidence ‘went missing’.
· Bought the shipyard two months after the closure: Alistair Fenwick.
· Attached, an old piece of Fenwick’s correspondence: ‘the donation needed for the file to be closed has been made.’
The file closed twenty-six years ago for ‘insufficient evidence’ was reopened.

· Cause of death: drowning.
· A round-edged blow to the back of the head; a wood splinter.
· No alcohol in the blood.
· Time of death: 22.00–23.00.

The marina canoe shed and the owner’s office (with the branch chief’s approval):

· On the shaft of the paddle of a canoe tied up the wrong way round, dried blood and a single long grey hair; Alistair Fenwick’s fingerprint on the paddle.
· In the office, four sample bottles taken from the victim’s home.
· Pacific Liaison Trust’s donation receipt: ‘on behalf of the Regional Coordinator’.
An unlit canoe comes from the marina side and pulls up to the victim’s deck.
The ranger sees the body and the canoe tied up the wrong way round.
The marina owner leaves through the gate on the card log.
Where did the victim’s sample bottles go?
I paint at night; the light is different.

I was painting around eleven. A canoe came across the water, from the marina side, unlit. It pulled up to Patricia’s deck. Talking, then a thud. I know I’m not on the gate log; I come home by canoe too, everyone does.
She wipes her brush with a rag, over and over.
What did you see last night?
It was recorded that the bottles were found in the office.
There were no bottles in the workshop.
The bottles weren’t in the river.
The death was ruled an accident; the marina grew.
Eloise Marr was arrested; the real canoe went back to the shed.
Alistair Fenwick was arrested; the marina’s expansion permit was suspended. The title ‘Regional Coordinator’ was written on the Footscray branch’s board.
Quoc Bui was arrested; the bottles stayed in the office.
There is a wood splinter in the blow to the back of the head; someone who slips isn’t struck with a paddle.
The neighbour saw the canoe and told you; the paddle and the bottles weren’t hers.
His fingerprint and the victim’s hair are on the paddle; the sample bottles are in his office. The gate log doesn’t clear him: the water side isn’t logged. The 2004 file shows why.
The former partner called her but wasn’t on the river that night; his print isn’t on the paddle.
I cleaned up this river. Nobody remembers.
The gate log is right there: I left at 19.42, nobody came in till morning. How could I have been there?

I went out through the gate and came back by canoe. I asked for the bottles; ‘You lost them in 2004 too; this time they won’t go missing,’ she said. The paddle was in my hand. The expansion permit was to be approved the next day; the coordinator had said, ‘We don’t want any hitches.’
I left at twenty to eight; my card’s on the log. Patricia was old, she slipped on the deck. Sad.
He takes his sunglasses from his collar and folds them.

Marina jetty gate, 8 November:

· 19.42 — exit (Alistair Fenwick’s card).
· No entries from 19.42 until 06.00.

Note: the gate is on the land side only. The marina’s hire canoes are moored on the water side and are not logged.
The river brings everything back, sooner or later.

I don’t do night patrols. But in the morning one of the marina’s hire canoes was tied up the wrong way round; Fenwick’s blokes never tie them like that. Last month Patricia and I took a sample from the marina’s outflow pipe. It was oily. She said, ‘Just like 2004.’
He coils the canoe rope in his hand.
Did you see anything on the river last night?
She had a heart attack and fell into the water
She was struck with a paddle and pushed into the water
A retired environmental engineer was found in the water beneath her houseboat; nobody came in through the marina gate.
40, the victim’s neighbour; a painter living on a houseboat.
57, marina owner on the banks of the Maribyrnong.
46, the victim’s former partner; boat repairer.
Our partnership was over. Our friendship wasn’t.

In 2004 Patricia and I put a file together: a shipyard dumping chemicals into the river. The file was closed, the shipyard was sold, and the buyer was Alistair Fenwick; he built the marina there. Patricia didn’t forget. I forgot; I needed the money. I rang her last night; she didn’t pick up.
He wipes his oily hands on his apron.

On the morning of 9 November 2030, on the Maribyrnong River, the retired environmental engineer Patricia Doyle-Hart (66) was found dead in the water beneath her houseboat.

The river ranger Jarrah Collins spotted the body from his patrol canoe at 06.20. The marina owner Alistair Fenwick said, ‘Nobody’s on the gate log; she must have fallen.’ Her neighbour, the painter Eloise Marr, and the victim’s former partner Quoc Bui are to be interviewed.
Request permission to open the 2004 file from the archive
Request permission to search the canoe shed
The gate log was a decoy: it didn’t count the water side. The neighbour told of the canoe, the former partner of 2004; the archive was opened, and the search found the paddle and the bottles.
Nobody came in through the gate. He came in from the river.

In 2004 the file on the shipyard that polluted the river was closed with a ‘donation’; Alistair Fenwick bought the shipyard and built a marina. Twenty-six years later Patricia Doyle-Hart took samples again. Fenwick left through the gate on the card log, came back across the water by canoe, demanded the bottles, and when she refused, struck her with the paddle.
Nobody — she slipped off the deck
The paddle of one of the marina’s hire canoes; a strand of the victim’s hair on the shaft.
The marina’s electronic gate log; no entries after 20.00.
Labelled water samples from the victim’s home; from the marina’s outflow.
